definition.text: Lincoln’s 1863 proposal for restoring former Confederate states to the Union, combining broad pardons with a requirement that 10% of the 1860 voting population swear loyalty and accept emancipation, after which states would draft new constitutions.

anchor.quote: In early December 1863, the president began the process of reunification by unveiling a three-part proposal known as the ten percent plan that outlined how the states would return.

facts.text: The plan included a general pardon, excluding high-ranking Confederate political and military leaders.

anchor.quote: The ten percent plan gave a general pardon to all Southerners except high-ranking Confederate government and military leaders;

facts.text: It required 10% of the 1860 voting population to take a binding oath of allegiance and support for emancipation.

anchor.quote: required 10 percent of the 1860 voting population in the former rebel states to take a binding oath of future allegiance to the United States and the emancipation of the enslaved;

facts.text: After the oath, the restored states would draft new state constitutions.

anchor.quote: declared that once those voters took those oaths, the restored Confederate states would draft new state constitutions.

facts.text: Lincoln’s approach was intentionally lenient, leaving 90% of 1860 voters not required to swear allegiance.

anchor.quote: Lincoln hoped that the leniency of the plan—90 percent of the 1860 voters did not have to swear allegiance to the Union or to emancipation—would bring about a quick and long-anticipated resolution and make emancipation more acceptable everywhere.

misconceptions.text: The Ten Percent Plan required most white Southern voters to swear loyalty before a state could rejoin the Union.
misconceptions.corrective: It required only 10% of the 1860 voting population to take the oath; Lincoln emphasized the plan’s leniency.

misconceptions.text: Lincoln’s plan focused primarily on punishing the South.
misconceptions.corrective: Lincoln proposed a “generous and non-punitive plan” intended to speed reunification.

kernels.term: Radical Republicans and the Wade–Davis Bill

definition.text: A congressional (Radical Republican) alternative to Lincoln’s Reconstruction approach that demanded harsher conditions for Southern political participation, including loyalty oaths that excluded many ex-Confederates; Lincoln blocked it with a pocket veto.

anchor.quote: Among other stipulations, the Wade-Davis Bill called for a majority of voters and government officials in Confederate states to take an oath, called the Ironclad Oath , swearing that they had never supported the Confederacy or made war against the United States.

facts.text: Radical Republicans wanted to punish the rebels and remake Southern society beyond what Lincoln proposed.

anchor.quote: These members of Congress, known as Radical Republicans , wanted to remake the South and punish the rebels.

facts.text: Radical Republicans insisted on harsh terms and protections for formerly enslaved people.

anchor.quote: Radical Republicans insisted on harsh terms for the defeated Confederacy and protection for formerly enslaved people, going far beyond what the president proposed.

facts.text: The Ironclad Oath would bar those unwilling/unable to swear they never supported the Confederacy from future political life.

anchor.quote: Those who could not or would not take the oath would be unable to take part in the future political life of the South.

facts.text: Lincoln killed the Wade–Davis Bill via pocket veto.

anchor.quote: The president refused to sign, using the pocket veto (that is, taking no action) to kill the bill.

facts.text: Lincoln believed the Wade–Davis criteria would prevent any Southern state from qualifying and delay Reconstruction.

anchor.quote: Lincoln understood that no Southern state would have met the criteria of the Wade-Davis Bill, and its passage would simply have delayed the reconstruction of the South.

misconceptions.text: The Wade–Davis Bill was more lenient than Lincoln’s plan.
misconceptions.corrective: It was harsher, requiring a majority to take the Ironclad Oath and excluding many from political participation.

definition.text: A constitutional amendment ratified in 1865 that permanently abolished slavery in the United States, resolving legal uncertainties left by wartime measures like the Emancipation Proclamation.

anchor.quote: In December 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment was officially ratified and added to the Constitution.

facts.text: The Emancipation Proclamation did not fully resolve the legal status of enslaved people or slavery.

anchor.quote: Despite the 1863 Emancipation Proclamation, the legal status of enslaved people and the institution of slavery remained unresolved.

facts.text: Republicans made abolition a top priority in the 1864 party platform, calling for an amendment to end slavery permanently.

anchor.quote: To deal with the remaining uncertainties, the Republican Party made the abolition of slavery a top priority by including the issue in its 1864 party platform.

facts.text: The proposed amendment passed the Senate in April 1864 and the House in January 1865.

anchor.quote: A proposed constitutional amendment passed the Senate in April 1864, and the House of Representatives concurred in January 1865.

facts.text: The amendment gained necessary support in the states, including in the South, and then was ratified.

anchor.quote: The amendment then made its way to the states, where it swiftly gained the necessary support, including in the South.

facts.text: It was the first amendment added since 1804 and permanently abolished slavery.

anchor.quote: The first amendment added to the Constitution since 1804, it overturned a centuries-old practice by permanently abolishing slavery.

misconceptions.text: The Emancipation Proclamation alone permanently ended slavery everywhere in the United States.
misconceptions.corrective: The text notes slavery’s legal status remained unresolved after 1863; the Thirteenth Amendment permanently abolished slavery.

definition.text: A set of 1867 laws that placed much of the former Confederacy under U.S. military administration, required new state constitutions and ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment, and used federal oversight to protect freedpeople and manage voter registration and elections.

anchor.quote: The 1867 Military Reconstruction Act, which encompassed the vision of Radical Republicans, set a new direction for Reconstruction in the South.

facts.text: The act divided ten southern states (excluding Tennessee) into five military districts and imposed martial law with a Union general commanding each district.

anchor.quote: The 1867 act divided the ten southern states that had yet to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment into five military districts (Tennessee had already been readmitted to the Union by this time and so was excluded from these acts). Martial law was imposed, and a Union general commanded each district.

facts.text: Federal troops and district commanders were tasked with protecting freedpeople.

anchor.quote: These generals and twenty thousand federal troops stationed in the districts were charged with protecting freed people.

facts.text: A supplementary act extended voting rights to freedmen age 21, and the military oversaw voter registration and elections.

anchor.quote: When a supplementary act extended the right to vote to all freed men of voting age (21 years old), the military in each district oversaw the elections and the registration of voters.

facts.text: States could rejoin the Union only after writing new constitutions and ratifying the Fourteenth Amendment.

anchor.quote: Only after new state constitutions had been written and states had ratified the Fourteenth Amendment could these states rejoin the Union.

facts.text: Johnson vetoed the Reconstruction Acts; Congress overrode the vetoes and by the end of 1870 the states under military rule had ratified the Fourteenth Amendment and been restored to the Union.

anchor.quote: Predictably, President Johnson vetoed the Reconstruction Acts, viewing them as both unnecessary and unconstitutional. Once again, Congress overrode Johnson’s vetoes, and by the end of 1870, all the southern states under military rule had ratified the Fourteenth Amendment and been restored to the Union

misconceptions.corrective: Tennessee was excluded because it had already been readmitted to the Union when the acts were passed.

misconceptions.text: Southern states automatically rejoined the Union once the Civil War ended, without meeting federal requirements.
misconceptions.corrective: The acts required new state constitutions and ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment before readmission.

definition.text: The 1868 constitutional process in which the House impeached President Andrew Johnson—largely over alleged violations of congressional authority (including the Tenure of Office Act)—and the Senate trial resulted in his acquittal by one vote short of the two-thirds requirement.

anchor.quote: The House of Representatives quickly drafted a resolution to impeach him, a first in American history.

facts.text: Congress passed the Command of the Army Act and the Tenure of Office Act (both described as of dubious constitutionality) to limit Johnson’s interference in Reconstruction.

anchor.quote: To that end, Radical Republicans passed two laws of dubious constitutionality.

facts.text: The Tenure of Office Act required Senate approval to appoint or remove officials.

anchor.quote: The Tenure of Office Act, which Congress passed in 1867, required the president to gain the approval of the Senate whenever he appointed or removed officials.

facts.text: Johnson removed Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton without Senate approval, prompting claims he violated the Tenure of Office Act.

anchor.quote: In August 1867, President Johnson removed Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton, who had aligned himself with the Radical Republicans, without gaining Senate approval.

facts.text: In impeachment, the House prosecutes and the Senate acts as judge deciding removal.

anchor.quote: In impeachment proceedings, the House of Representatives serves as the prosecution and the Senate acts as judge, deciding whether the president should be removed from office

facts.text: Johnson was acquitted in the Senate by a vote of 35 to 19, one vote short of the two-thirds majority needed to convict.

anchor.quote: the final vote was 35 to 19, one vote short of the required two-thirds majority.

definition.text: The Reconstruction-era constitutional amendment ratified in 1870 that prohibited denying or abridging the right to vote on the basis of race, color, or previous condition of servitude, but left loopholes that did not explicitly address tools like literacy tests and poll taxes.

anchor.quote: With the Fifteenth Amendment, they sought to correct this major weakness by finally extending to Black men the right to vote.

facts.text: The amendment states that voting rights cannot be denied or abridged because of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.

anchor.quote: The amendment directed that "[t]he right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude."

facts.text: To gain broad support, the amendment excluded language addressing literacy tests and poll taxes, common methods of disenfranchisement.

anchor.quote: As part of a compromise to ensure the passage of the amendment with the broadest possible support, drafters of the amendment specifically excluded language that addressed literacy tests and poll taxes

facts.text: Charles Sumner refused to vote for the amendment because it did not address loopholes.

anchor.quote: Charles Sumner of Massachusetts, himself an ardent supporter of legal equality without exception to race, refused to vote for the amendment precisely because it did not address these obvious loopholes.

facts.text: The amendment provided for universal manhood suffrage and identified Black men, including formerly enslaved men, as deserving the vote.

anchor.quote: Despite these weaknesses, the language of the amendment did provide for universal manhood suffrage—the right of all men to vote—and crucially identified Black men, including those who had been enslaved, as deserving the right to vote.

facts.text: It was ratified in 1870 and many believed it secured formerly enslaved people’s rights.

anchor.quote: This, the third and final of the Reconstruction amendments, was ratified in 1870 ( Figure 16.9 ).

definition.text: An ideology that framed U.S. continental expansion as divinely sanctioned and historically inevitable, used to promote and justify westward settlement and governance over peoples encountered in the West.

anchor.quote: This phrase, which implies divine encouragement for territorial expansion, was coined by magazine editor John O’Sullivan in 1845

facts.text: John O’Sullivan coined the term in 1845 and tied it to Providence and continental expansion.

anchor.quote: was coined by magazine editor John O’Sullivan in 1845, when he wrote in the United States Magazine and Democratic Review that “it was our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our multiplying millions.”

facts.text: Although first invoked regarding Texas, the idea later promoted westward settlement through the nineteenth century.

anchor.quote: Although the context of O’Sullivan’s original article was to encourage expansion into the newly acquired Texas territory, the spirit it invoked would subsequently be used to encourage westward settlement throughout the rest of the nineteenth century.

facts.text: Economic interests (such as land developers and railroad investors) promoted Manifest Destiny to encourage settlement for profit.

anchor.quote: Land developers, railroad magnates, and other investors capitalized on the notion to encourage westward settlement for their own financial benefit.

facts.text: A core claim was that Americans were destined (even divinely ordained) to expand democratic institutions across the continent.

anchor.quote: Americans were destined—and indeed divinely ordained—to expand democratic institutions throughout the continent.

facts.text: Manifest Destiny functioned as a justification that shaped how Americans viewed their right and duty to govern other groups and excuse harsh tactics.

anchor.quote: Manifest Destiny justified in Americans’ minds their right and duty to govern any other groups they encountered during their expansion, as well as absolved them of any questionable tactics they employed in the process.

misconceptions.text: Manifest Destiny was only a neutral description of population growth and settlement.
misconceptions.corrective: In the text it is presented as an ideology implying divine sanction and used to justify governing other groups and excusing tactics during expansion.

misconceptions.text: The West was essentially empty, so expansion only meant moving into unused land.
misconceptions.corrective: The section notes that Hispanic communities, diverse tribes, and other settlers already lived in many regions, making expansion a complex exchange rather than filling empty space.

kernels.term: Federal government assistance to westward migration (1862)

definition.text: A set of federal policies and on-the-ground actions that lowered barriers to moving west by distributing land, supporting railroad construction, and providing military infrastructure such as forts.

anchor.quote: To assist the settlers in their move westward and transform the migration from a trickle into a steady flow, Congress passed two significant pieces of legislation in 1862: the Homestead Act and the Pacific Railway Act.

facts.text: Congress passed the Homestead Act and Pacific Railway Act in 1862 to increase westward migration.

anchor.quote: Congress passed two significant pieces of legislation in 1862: the Homestead Act and the Pacific Railway Act.

facts.text: The Homestead Act offered 160 acres for a nominal filing fee to heads of household or individuals over twenty-one, including unmarried women.

anchor.quote: The Homestead Act allowed any head of household, or individual over the age of twenty-one—including unmarried women—to receive a parcel of 160 acres for only a nominal filing fee.

facts.text: Homesteaders had to “improve the land” within five years, with minimal standards such as clearing acres, building small structures, or keeping livestock.

anchor.quote: All that recipients were required to do in exchange was to “improve the land” within a period of five years of taking possession. The standards for improvement were minimal: Owners could clear a few acres, build small houses or barns, or maintain livestock.

facts.text: The Homestead Act transferred more than 270 million acres of public land to private citizens.

anchor.quote: Under this act, the government transferred over 270 million acres of public domain land to private citizens.

facts.text: The Pacific Railway Act commissioned the Union Pacific and Central Pacific to build toward each other, and provided land grants and bonds that enabled profits and completion of the first transcontinental railroad in 1869.

facts.text: The Oregon Trail was about two thousand miles long and became commonly used by wagon trains by the 1840s.

anchor.quote: The Oregon Trail is the most famous of these western routes. Two thousand miles long and barely passable on foot in the early nineteenth century, by the 1840s, wagon trains were a common sight.

facts.text: Between 1845 and 1870, over 400,000 settlers traveled west from Missouri on the Oregon Trail.

definition.text: In the late nineteenth century, railroads became the nation’s first large-scale corporate industry, rapidly expanding track mileage and enabling national movement of raw materials and finished goods, which accelerated growth across many other industries.

anchor.quote: The railroad industry quickly became the nation’s first “big business.”

facts.text: By 1890, railroads reached nearly every part of the United States and connected raw materials to factories and finished goods to markets.

anchor.quote: By 1890, railroad lines covered nearly every corner of the United States, bringing raw materials to industrial factories and finished goods to consumer markets.

facts.text: Track mileage increased dramatically from the end of the Civil War to the end of the century.

anchor.quote: The amount of track grew from 35,000 miles at the end of the Civil War to over 200,000 miles by the close of the century.

definition.text: “Robber barons” was a negative label for wealthy industrialists—especially railroad owners—accused of using exploitative or shady methods; a key example was differential shipping rates that favored large shippers over local farmers and producers.

kernels.term: Farmers’ Revolt: economic causes (overproduction, tariffs, currency)

definition.text: A set of late-nineteenth-century economic pressures on U.S. farmers—especially falling prices from overproduction, higher costs from tariffs, and tight money under gold-focused policy—that helped drive farmers toward collective protest and reform politics.

anchor.loc: 20.3 Farmers Revolt in the Populist Era (opening paragraphs)
anchor.quote: The challenges that many American farmers faced in the last quarter of the nineteenth century were significant. They contended with economic hardships born out of rapidly declining farm prices, prohibitively high tariffs on items they needed to purchase, and foreign competition. One of the largest challenges they faced was overproduction, where the glut of their products in the marketplace drove the price lower and lower.

facts.text: Overproduction was intensified by homestead expansion and new industrial farm tools that increased yields.

anchor.quote: Overproduction of crops occurred in part due to the westward expansion of homestead farms and in part because industrialization led to new farm tools that dramatically increased crop yields.

facts.text: Farmers often responded to debt by producing more, which pushed prices down further—a self-reinforcing cycle.

anchor.quote: As farmers fell deeper into debt, whether it be to the local stores where they bought supplies or to the railroads that shipped their produce, their response was to increase crop production each year in the hope of earning more money with which to pay back their debt. The more they produced, the lower prices dropped.

facts.text: Tariffs raised the cost of industrial goods farmers bought, but did not raise farm prices in the same way.

anchor.quote: Rising tariffs on industrial products made purchased items more expensive, yet tariffs were not being used to keep farm prices artificially high as well. Therefore, farmers were paying inflated prices but not receiving them.

facts.text: Many farmers pushed for more money in circulation (paper or silver) to create inflationary pressure that would raise farm prices.

anchor.quote: Farmers needed more money in circulation, whether it was paper or silver, in order to create inflationary pressure. Inflationary pressure would allow farm prices to increase, thus allowing them to earn more money that they could then spend on the higher-priced goods in stores.

definition.text: An early farmer organizing movement (the Grange) that promoted cooperatives and briefly achieved state-level regulation (Granger Laws) and currency-focused politics (Greenback Party), but faced legal limits and declined by the late 1880s.

anchor.quote: One of the first efforts to organize farmers came in 1867 with Oliver Hudson Kelly’s creation of the Patrons of Husbandry, more popularly known as the Grange .

anchor.quote: In the wake of the Civil War, the Grangers quickly grew to over 1.5 million members in less than a decade

definition.text: The emergence of one-party totalitarian regimes in Italy and Germany amid post–World War I instability and economic crisis, in which leaders dismantled democratic institutions and expanded state power through nationalism, militarism, and anti-Communism.

facts.text: As World War II ended, the U.S.–Soviet alliance broke down because each side believed its political and economic system was superior and their visions for Europe and the world were incompatible.

definition.text: A conservative political turn associated with Ronald Reagan’s 1980 election and governing agenda, framing “big government” and social reform as the problem and setting policy priorities that shaped later U.S. politics.

anchor.quote: Leading the so-called Reagan Revolution, he appealed to voters with the promise that the principles of conservatism could halt and revert the social and economic changes of the last generation.

facts.text: Reagan argued that big government and social reform efforts were the problem rather than the solution.

anchor.quote: Reagan won the White House by citing big government and attempts at social reform as the problem, not the solution.

facts.text: His appeal included moderates and conservatives worried about social change and perceived decline in U.S. influence.

anchor.quote: He appealed to moderates and conservatives anxious about social change and the seeming loss of American power and influence on the world stage.

facts.text: Reagan’s election occurred amid the growth of the New Right.

anchor.loc: Republicans Back in the White House
anchor.quote: His victory was the result of a combination of dissatisfaction with the presidential leadership of Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter in the 1970s and the growth of the New Right .

facts.text: The New Right included evangelical Christians organized around issues like abortion, feminism, and sex education.

anchor.loc: Republicans Back in the White House
anchor.quote: Many were evangelical Christians, like those who joined Jerry Falwell’s Moral Majority, and opposed the legalization of abortion, the feminist movement, and sex education in public schools.

facts.text: The 1980 election saw low turnout, and those who voted were disproportionately older, White, and wealthier.

anchor.loc: Republicans Back in the White House
anchor.quote: Only 52 percent of eligible voters went to the polls in 1980, the lowest turnout for a presidential election since 1948.

misconceptions.text: The Reagan Revolution describes only Reagan’s personality and communication style, not substantive political change.
misconceptions.corrective: It refers to a conservative agenda and voter coalition that shaped policy priorities and the broader political landscape.

misconceptions.text: Reagan won in 1980 because overall voter participation was unusually high and broadly representative.
misconceptions.corrective: Turnout was low, and the electorate was skewed: “older, Whiter, and wealthier than those who did not vote.”

definition.text: Reagan-era economic policy emphasizing tax cuts (especially at the top), deregulation, and anti-inflation measures, justified by supply-side theory that incentives for investment would produce growth and jobs.

anchor.quote: His economic policies, called Reaganomics by the press, were based on a theory called supply-side economics, about which many economists were skeptical.

facts.text: The policy logic emphasized cutting taxes at the top to motivate investment with downstream job creation.

anchor.quote: Reagan cut income taxes for those at the top of the economic ladder, which was supposed to motivate the rich to invest in businesses, factories, and the stock market in anticipation of high returns.

facts.text: Supporters argued growth would increase total tax revenue even at lower tax rates.

anchor.quote: Economic growth would also increase the total tax revenue—even at a lower tax rate.

facts.text: Reaganomics also included deregulation and higher interest rates to control inflation, though these initiatives began under Carter.

anchor.quote: Reaganomics also included the deregulation of industry and higher interest rates to control inflation, but these initiatives preceded Reagan and were conceived in the Carter administration.

facts.text: Congress passed the Economic Recovery Tax Act in 1981, phasing in a 25 percent overall tax reduction over three years.

anchor.quote: On July 29, 1981, Congress passed the Economic Recovery Tax Act, which phased in a 25 percent overall reduction in taxes over a period of three years.

facts.text: Despite tax cuts, government spending was not reduced, and federal employment increased during Reagan’s time in office.

anchor.quote: Reagan was successful at cutting taxes, but he failed to reduce government spending.

misconceptions.text: Reaganomics mainly targeted tax relief for low-income Americans.
misconceptions.corrective: The section emphasizes cutting income taxes “for those at the top of the economic ladder” as a key mechanism.

misconceptions.text: Reaganomics was entirely new in 1981, including the anti-inflation high-interest-rate approach.
misconceptions.corrective: The text states deregulation and higher interest rates to control inflation “preceded Reagan” and were “conceived in the Carter administration.”

definition.text: A pivotal labor relations episode in which Reagan fired striking federal air traffic controllers, destroying PATCO and signaling a shift toward replacing striking workers, contributing to weakened unions.

anchor.quote: in 1981, the president fired twelve thousand federal air traffic controllers who had gone on strike to secure better working conditions (which would also have improved the public’s safety).

facts.text: Reagan’s action effectively destroyed PATCO.

anchor.quote: His action effectively destroyed the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (PATCO)

facts.text: The episode helped usher in an era in which employers replaced striking workers.

facts.text: The administration sought to weaken the power of labor unions as part of its broader approach.

anchor.quote: But Reagan seemed less flexible when it came to deregulating industry and weakening the power of labor unions.

facts.text: Union weakening contributed to the leveling off of real wages for the average American family during the 1980s.

anchor.quote: The weakening of unions contributed to the leveling off of real wages for the average American family during the 1980s.

definition.text: A post-9/11 U.S. foreign-policy stance asserting the U.S. right to protect itself from terrorism through pre-emptive war and by removing hostile governments in favor of friendly (preferably democratic) regimes.

anchor.quote: This speech encapsulated what became known as the Bush Doctrine , the belief that the United States has the right to protect itself from terrorist acts by engaging in pre-emptive wars or ousting hostile governments in favor of friendly, preferably democratic, regimes.

facts.text: After 9/11, President Bush told Congress the U.S. would bring those responsible to justice and framed U.S. policy as a war on terrorism.

anchor.quote: That evening, President Bush promised the nation that those responsible for the attacks would be brought to justice.

facts.text: Congress authorized the president to use all means necessary against those involved in the 9/11 attacks.

anchor.quote: Three days later, Congress issued a joint resolution authorizing the president to use all means necessary against the individuals, organizations, or nations involved in the attacks.

facts.text: Bush blamed al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden and demanded the Taliban hand him over or face U.S. attack.

anchor.quote: Bush declared war on terrorism, blamed al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden for the attacks, and demanded that the radical Islamic fundamentalists who ruled Afghanistan, the Taliban , turn bin Laden over or face attack by the United States.

facts.text: The policy included the idea of pre-emptive war and regime change in the name of self-protection from terrorist acts.

anchor.quote: engaging in pre-emptive wars or ousting hostile governments in favor of friendly, preferably democratic, regimes.

misconceptions.text: The Bush Doctrine only meant retaliating after an attack had already occurred.
misconceptions.corrective: In the text, the doctrine is explicitly tied to "pre-emptive wars" and "ousting hostile governments" as forms of self-protection.

misconceptions.text: The Bush Doctrine was only about Afghanistan and had nothing to do with broader U.S. strategy.
misconceptions.corrective: The definition frames it as a general belief about U.S. rights and tools (pre-emption and regime change), not a single-country policy.

examples.text: Explaining how the Bush Doctrine justified action against governments seen as harboring or supporting terrorists.

definition.text: A coordinated terrorist operation on September 11, 2001 in which al-Qaeda hijackers seized four U.S. airliners, struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, and caused a fourth plane to crash in Pennsylvania after passengers intervened.

anchor.quote: Shortly after takeoff on the morning of September 11, 2001, teams of hijackers from the Islamist terrorist group al-Qaeda seized control of four American airliners.

facts.text: Two hijacked planes were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan.

anchor.quote: Two of the airplanes were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan.

facts.text: Both towers collapsed within two hours due to crash heat and burning jet fuel, becoming rubble.

anchor.quote: Less than two hours later, the heat from the crash and the explosion of jet fuel caused the upper floors of both buildings to collapse onto the lower floors, reducing both towers to smoldering rubble.

facts.text: The Pentagon attack killed everyone on board the plane and 125 people on the ground.

anchor.quote: The third hijacked plane was flown into the Pentagon building in northern Virginia, just outside Washington, DC, killing everyone on board and 125 people on the ground.

facts.text: The fourth plane crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania after passengers tried to storm the cockpit; all aboard died.

anchor.quote: The fourth plane, also heading towards Washington, crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, when passengers, aware of the other attacks, attempted to storm the cockpit and disarm the hijackers. Everyone on board was killed

definition.text: The 2003 U.S.-led coalition invasion of Iraq launched after the United States cut off relations with Iraq, justified publicly in part by fears about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction and claims of UN resolution violations.

anchor.quote: Two days later, in a coalition with Great Britain, Australia, and Poland, the United States began “Operation Iraqi Freedom” with an invasion of Iraq.

facts.text: A faction in the Bush administration labeled neoconservatives pushed for striking Iraq in the wake of 9/11; others like Colin Powell were more cautious.

anchor.quote: A faction within the Bush administration, sometimes labeled neoconservatives, believed Iraq’s recalcitrance in the face of overwhelming U.S. military superiority represented a dangerous symbol to terrorist groups around the world

facts.text: A key argument for invasion was fear that Saddam Hussein was stockpiling weapons of mass destruction (nuclear, chemical, or biological).

anchor.quote: The immediate impetus to the invasion, it argued, was the fear that Hussein was stockpiling weapons of mass destruction ( WMDs ): nuclear, chemical, or biological weapons capable of wreaking great havoc.

facts.text: Hans Blix dismissed U.S. claims of Iraqi WMD possession, arguing Iraq did not appear to have WMDs.

anchor.quote: Hans Blix, dismissed these claims. Blix argued that while Saddam Hussein was not being entirely forthright, he did not appear to be in possession of WMDs.

facts.text: The U.S. began the invasion after cutting off relations with Iraq and building a coalition including Great Britain, Australia, and Poland.

anchor.quote: On March 17, 2003, the United States cut off all relations with Iraq. Two days later, in a coalition with Great Britain, Australia, and Poland

facts.text: Though early military progress seemed smooth, the U.S. was not prepared for long occupation and conflict, making the 2003 victory celebration premature by more than seven years.

anchor.quote: Thus, even though Bush proclaimed a U.S. victory in May 2003, on the deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln with the banner “Mission Accomplished” prominently displayed behind him, the celebration proved premature by more than seven years
